title: Use the same measurement protocol
question: What do a moving clock and rod actually report?
recap: For an inertially moving clock, its own elapsed time is smaller than the coordinate interval between its ticks. A moving rod’s simultaneous coordinate length is smaller than its rest length; neither result is a photographic distortion.
premises: Use an ideal clock and inertial rod, with the appropriate event pairs.
γ uses the relative inertial speed in the specified frame.
limitations: Reciprocal moving-clock rates compare different distant-clock procedures.
A single transformed event separation is not automatically a length or clock reading.

overview.text: For an inertially moving clock, its own elapsed time is smaller than the coordinate interval between its ticks. A moving rod’s simultaneous coordinate length is smaller than its rest length; neither result is a photographic distortion.

full.spoken: Coordinate time between a moving clock’s ticks is gamma times its proper elapsed time; simultaneous moving-rod length is rest length over gamma.

full.text: At 0.6c, a clock experiences 0.8 seconds during a one-second coordinate interval. A rod of rest length 1 metre has simultaneous coordinate length 0.8 metre. Their shared factor follows from different event constraints.

For the clock, use ticks at the same place in its rest frame. For the rod, set the endpoint measurement times equal in the measuring frame. SR-03 and SR-05 let the reader inspect those constraints separately.

full.spoken: At small speed, the clock’s fractional loss per coordinate second approaches one half v squared over c squared.

full.returnCaption: Return to what do a moving clock and rod actually report.

items: Specify which clock supplies each time reading.
For a clock’s own ticks, use its worldline and the frame where it is locally at rest.
For a moving length, impose simultaneity in the measuring frame.
At 0.6c compute γ = 1.25 and its inverse 0.8.
Keep the exact loss 0.2 distinct from the second-order approximation 0.18 at that speed.

margin.text: The light clock is a later teaching construction. The printed second-order clock-loss approximation is not an exact formula at arbitrary speed.
